initial_requirements: MultiMahjong is a computer version of Mahjong for both networked and standalone play. Up to four people should be able to join a shared game through client applications connected to a game server. When fewer human players are available, the application should provide computer-controlled opponents so that a user can still start and complete a valid game.

messages.content: Hello, I’m GPTREI, your requirements elicitation assistant. I’ll be gathering detailed information about MultiMahjong to make sure we capture the needed requirements clearly and completely. Before we begin, are you in line with the scope of this interview, or do your expectations differ?

Yes, that sounds in line with what we’re trying to capture. I’m here to help define the MultiMahjong game experience for both networked and standalone play, including how human and computer players fit together. If anything comes up that’s outside the current scope, I’ll say so and we can decide whether it belongs in this phase.
To start off, could you please introduce yourself and your connection to this project?

I’m speaking as the stakeholder representing the product side of MultiMahjong, so I’m focused on what the game needs to do for players and how it should work at a practical level. My interest is in making sure we capture the core gameplay, multiplayer setup, and the computer-opponent fallback clearly enough for development.
Thank you. Could you please describe MultiMahjong in two to four sentences?

MultiMahjong is a computer-based Mahjong game that supports both networked multiplayer and standalone play. Up to four players can join the same game through client applications connected to a game server, and when there aren’t enough human players, the system should fill the remaining seats with computer-controlled opponents. The goal is for a user to still be able to start and complete a valid game even if they’re playing alone.
Can you describe the current process or system you use for setting up and playing a Mahjong game, if there is one?

Right now, there isn’t a single existing system we rely on for this project. In practice, people either play Mahjong physically or use different digital versions depending on what’s available, but for MultiMahjong we’re defining the setup and play flow from scratch. The main expectation is that it should be straightforward for players to join a game, and for a solo user to start a match without needing to manage the missing seats manually.
What current processes do you want to change or improve, or what features do you hope to get from this project?

We want to make it easy to start and complete a Mahjong game whether or not a full group of people is available. The biggest improvement is having the game automatically support up to four players and fill empty spots with computer opponents when needed, so a user doesn’t get stuck waiting for others. We also want the networked version to let people connect through clients to a shared game server without the setup feeling complicated.

So the main features are: networked play through client applications connected to a shared game server, standalone play, and automatic computer opponents to fill empty seats so a valid game can always be completed, right?
Yes, that’s right. Those are the core features we want for MultiMahjong.
Are there any other features you would like to see in this project, perhaps something that has not been the primary focus so far?

Nothing major has been decided beyond the core gameplay and multiplayer support. If we add anything else, it would likely be quality-of-life features, but I’d need to check with the team before saying more.

Based on your description, should we also include a way for players to choose whether computer opponents fill missing seats automatically or only when the host starts a game with fewer than four humans?

I think that would be useful, yes. My preference is that the host should have control over whether the missing seats are filled automatically or whether the game waits until they choose to start with computer players. That said, I’d want to confirm the exact behavior with the team, because we haven’t fully settled that detail.
Which of these would you prioritize first: networked multiplayer setup, standalone play, automatic computer-opponent filling, or host control over when computer players are added?

I’d prioritize standalone play and automatic computer-opponent filling first, because that guarantees a user can actually start and finish a game on their own. After that, I’d focus on the networked multiplayer setup, since that’s the main shared-play experience. Host control over when computer players are added sounds useful, but I’d treat it as lower priority unless the team feels strongly about it.
Please elaborate on what you want standalone play to accomplish.

Standalone play should let one person launch the game locally and play a complete Mahjong match without needing any network connection or other human players. If there aren’t enough people, the system should automatically supply computer opponents so the game is still valid and playable from start to finish. The main goal is convenience and reliability, so someone can open the app and immediately get a full game experience.
Could you describe how the game should behave when fewer than four human players are available in standalone play?

When fewer than four humans are available, the game should still let the player start, and it should fill the remaining seats with computer-controlled opponents. Those opponents should behave well enough that the match can proceed normally and finish as a valid game. I’d expect that to happen automatically in standalone play, since the whole point is not to block the user from playing.
Could you describe how the game should behave when fewer than four human players are available in networked play?

In networked play, I’d still want the game to be able to start even if not all four seats are human. The server should allow computer-controlled opponents to fill the missing spots so the session can proceed as a complete game. If there’s a host, I’d expect them to be able to see that the game is being padded with AI players, but the exact control over that may still need confirmation.
Who else do you think has valuable insights into the project, whose needs should be considered, and why?

The most important people besides the core players would be the host or person setting up the game, because they decide when a session starts and whether missing seats are acceptable. I’d also want input from whoever is responsible for maintaining the game server, since networked play and AI seat-filling will affect how reliable and easy it is to run. If we’re thinking about polish, someone from testing or support would probably have useful feedback too, because they’ll see where players get confused or blocked.
What would you consider a successful deployment of MultiMahjong?

A successful deployment would be one where a player can install or access the app, start a Mahjong game either alone or with others, and complete a full match without major setup issues. For the networked side, it would mean multiple clients can connect to the server reliably and play together, with computer opponents filling any missing seats as needed. I’d also consider it successful if the experience is stable enough that people can actually use it repeatedly without the game getting stuck or failing to start.

To summarize, we discussed standalone play that lets a single user start and complete a full Mahjong match locally, automatic computer-opponent filling to replace missing human players, networked multiplayer through clients connected to a shared server, and a lower-priority host control for when AI players are added. Success means users can reliably start, join, and finish games without setup issues or the game getting stuck. Is there anything else you would like to add?

That summary sounds right to me. The only thing I’d add is that the AI players should be good enough to keep the game moving naturally, not just fill seats in a way that feels broken or confusing. Beyond that, I think we’ve covered the main needs for now.
